query: What exact hierarchical Bayesian model specification (likelihoods, fixed effects, random effects, hyperpriors with parameter values) is recommended for small-group gendered-language inference?

response.query: What exact hierarchical Bayesian model specification (likelihoods, fixed effects, random effects, hyperpriors with parameter values) is recommended for small-group gendered-language inference?
response.answer: For small-group gendered-language inference, use a Bayesian hierarchical model with fixed effects for gender and random effects for group-level intercepts, with normal priors for fixed effects and inverse-gamma for random effects' variance.

results.title: Implementing Bayesian Hierarchical Modeling
results.content: # Implementing Bayesian Hierarchical Modeling. Bayesian hierarchical modeling is a powerful approach to statistical analysis that allows you to incorporate both individual-level variability and complex structured dependencies between observations. By integrating probability theory with data, hierarchical models provide a robust framework for drawing inferences in diverse applications, from medical studies to marketing research. This article provides a comprehensive guide to implementing Bayesian hierarchical models in Python using PyMC3 and Stan, complete with code examples, model diagnostics, and real-world case studies. * How to set up your Python environment for Bayesian modeling. * Techniques for specifying hierarchical models, including defining pooling structures and selecting appropriate priors. ### Overview of PyMC3 and Stan Both PyMC3 and Stan are widely used for Bayesian inference: - **PyMC3**: A Python library that leverages Theano/NumPy backend for building complex probabilistic models using intuitive Python code. flowchart TD A["Data Collection"] --> B["Model Specification"] B --> C["PyMC3"] B --> D["Stan"] C --> E["Sampling"] D --> F["Sampling"] E --> G["Diagnostics"] F --> G["Diagnostics"] G --> H["Model Optimization & Inference"]. Hierarchical models, also known as multi-level models, allow the modeling of data that are grouped or nested. In Bayesian hierarchical modeling, parameters can be introduced at different levels:. PyMC3 offers a high-level syntax to construct and sample from Bayesian models. Below is a simple code example for a hierarchical model in PyMC3 applied to a hypothetical dataset:. Bayesian hierarchical modeling offers a flexible and robust framework for managing complex, multi-level data. * Formulating hierarchical models by defining levels, pooling structures, and selecting priors/hyperpriors. * Developing hierarchical Bayesian models in both PyMC3 and Stan with code examples. * Real-world case studies on medical data and marketing campaign analysis, demonstrating the practical benefits of hierarchical models. Adopting Bayesian hierarchical models in your workflow can significantly improve the robustness of statistical inference, particularly in scenarios with nested or grouped data. - Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models (ARM). 7. Hierarchical Bayesian Modeling for Marketing Data (ScienceDirect). With this comprehensive guide, you’re well-prepared to start implementing Bayesian hierarchical models in practice. Whether you choose PyMC3 or Stan, the key is to understand your data, choose appropriate priors, and iteratively diagnose and optimize your models for reliable inference.

results.title: Chapter 2 The Model Matrix and Random Effects | Bayesian Hierarchical Models in Ecology
results.content: # Chapter 2 The Model Matrix and Random Effects. Recall that the linear contribution to our model includes the predictors (explanatory variables) with additive effects. This model is considering snake mass to be made up of these components: the mean snake mass, the region effect, and the residual error. These two parameterizations really only come into play when you have a categorical variable—the representation of continuous variables in the model matrix includes the quantity or magnitude of that variable (and defaults to an effects parameterization). The model matrix for this model (an effect parameterization) can be reported as such. ## 2.2 Model Effects. To understand hierarchical models, we need to understand random effects, and to understand random effects, we need to understand **variance**. Random effects are those model effects that can be thought of as units from a distribution, almost like a random variable. + Several reasons why random effects extract more informationvfrom your data and model. + Built-in safety: with no real group-level information, effects revert back to a fixed effects model (essentially). Do I need a random effect (hierarchical model)? Random Effects Equation Notation There will be a much more extensive treatment of model notation and you will need to become familari with notation to successfully code models; however, now is as good a time as any to introduce some basics of random effects statistical notation. Because random effects are used to model variation at different levels of the data, they add a hierarchical structure to the model. Let’s start with non-hierarchical models and review how data inform parameters. In cases like these, we can structure a model where the data inform factor level parameters, but those factor level parameters are then governed by some additional parameter (Figure 2.5). “Multilevel (hierarchical) modeling is a generalization of linear and generalized linear modeling in which regression coeffcients are themselves given a model, whose parameters are also estimated from data.” Gelman and Hill (2006). The implicit process model is commonly represented by a collection of random effects that are often spatially and or temporally indexed. Similarly, plenty of statistical models applied in ecology have at least one set of random effects (beyond the residual) and therefore represent a hierarchical model.

results.title: What do "Fixed Effects" and "Random Effects" mean to you? - General - PyMC Discourse
results.content: 1. Fixed Effects are constant across individuals, and random effects vary. 2. Effects are fixed if they are interesting in themselves or random if there is an interest in the underlying population. 3. Fixed effects are estimated from large samples, random effects from small samples. 4. Random effects are realizations of random variables. 5. Fixed effects are estimated using maximum likelihood, random effects exhibit shrinkage. There, fixed effects are group specific intercepts, and random effects are something like a clustered standard error adjustment. * Terminology: "hierarchical", "multi-level", "mixed effect", "partially pooled" models - is it all the same? ## post by ricardoV94 on Dec 5, 2024. Those are the fixed and random effects, respectively, of definition 1. ## post by bwengals on Dec 5, 2024. I’m gonna be a contrarian and say I very much like the fixed / random terminology. **Random effect:** Synonymous with a hierarchical model. The hospital effect is a random effect because the 5 hospitals in the data is a random sample from an infinite number of hospitals. **Fixed effect:** The effect is “fixed” by the experimenter. This is a fixed effect because you want to measure the effect of drug A, drug B and drug C independently. You don’t use a hierarchical model / partial pooling because it would be a bad idea to think about the three drugs as some random sample from an infinite number of different drugs. You want to treat each drug effect (that the experimenter fixed in advance) independently. * Definition 5: fixed effects *can* be estimated with maximum likelihood just fine, while random effects *do* exhibit shrinkage, so that’s true. * Definition 4: Yes, random effects (the observed groups), are realizations of random variables (the population), so I think that’s true too. You don’t really care about the hospital effect, it’s a nuisance variable. * Definition 1: The same drugs A, B, C are used across all 5 hospitals. Also possible that I have retconned the fixed and random effects terminology into something that makes sense only to me? Fixed = not hierarchical, no pooling, effects are independent. ## post by jaharvey8 on Dec 5, 2024.

results.title: bayesian - What is the Frequentist definition of fixed effects? - Cross Validated
results.content: Under a Bayesian approach, a fixed effect is one where we estimate each parameter (e.g., the mean for each species within a genus) independently (with independently specified priors), while for a random effect the parameters for each level are modeled as being drawn from a distribution (usually Normal); in standard statistical notation, $\textrm{species\_mean} \sim {\cal N}(\textrm{genus\_mean}, \sigma^2\_{\textrm{species}})$. Bolker's chapter thus provides clear Bayesian and Frequentist definitions of random effects, and a clear Bayesian definition of fixed effects. * $\begingroup$ I've edited the OP to clarify that I'm hoping for a definition consistent with @ben-bolker's Bayesian definitions of fixed/random effects and his Frequentist definition of random effects. (Indeed, any generally useful concept will have many different characterizations.) If you want a clear definition, then look at the mathematics: a fixed effect is unambiguously defined by the model in which it appears. This is the same for the Bayesian and Frequentist approach, which in principle do not differ in their way to describe a probability for the observations $Y\_{ij}$ conditional on the model parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ and independent variables $X\_{ij}$, where $Z\_i$ and $\epsilon\_j$ describe a non-deterministic part. So if you like, you could say that a frequentist definition of a fixed effect is: **'a model parameter that describes the deterministic part in a statistical model'**. How I interpret the question's description/definition of the difference in random effect and fixed effect in the Bayesian framework is more as something pragmatic than as some principle. * and the random effects are like *"for a random effect the parameters for each level are modeled as being drawn from a distribution"* (for each observation category $i$ a different random effect is 'drawn' from the distribution, e.g. the mean of a species is a model parameter that is considered different for each species). In a frequentist framework the fixed effect model parameters are not considered as random parameters, or at least it doesn't matter for the inference whether the parameters are a random parameter or not and it is left out the analysis. $\begingroup$ Basically, the difference between fixed effect and random effect is whether a parameter is considered fixed within the experiment or not. What is the difference between fixed effect, random effect in mixed effect models?

results.content: In this chapter, we’ll look at how to perform analysis and regressions using Bayesian techniques using **Bambi**, which stands for *BAyesian Model-Building Interface*. ## Bayesian Models via Formulae with Bambi#. Let’s see how to specify the model we did in Bayesian Inference only using **Bambi**. # True parameter values alpha_true, beta_true, sigma_true = 1,2.5,1.5 # Size of dataset size = 100 num_samples = 1000 num_chains = 2# Predictor variable: random sample X = prng. standard_normal(size) # Simulate outcome variable Y = alpha_true + beta_true* X + prng. Model("Y ~ X", df_bambi) # Fit the model using 1000 on each of 4 chains results = model. Note that the same set of variables as we saw in the first example are just appearing with different names here—the true values are an intercept of 1, a coefficient on \(X\) of 2.5, and a standard deviation of 1.5 (the variable `Y_sigma`) above. Model("Y ~ X + C(D)", data = df_bambi_cat) model_cat. from bambi import Prior prior ={"D": Prior("Normal", mu =0.5, sigma = 10)} model_cat = bmb. Model("Y ~ X + C(D)", data = df_bambi_cat, priors = prior) results_cat = model_cat. ### Mixed Effects Models in Bambi#. Here we use the Bambi model-building interface to quickly re-analyse the RRR data using a Bayesian approach and making use of random effects and fixed effects. Model("value ~ condition + age + gender", df_rrr, dropna = True). # Fixed effects and group specific (or random) intercepts for study model_rrr = bmb. Model("value ~ condition + age + gender + (1|study)", df_rrr, dropna = True) model_rrr. **Bambi** has chosen to draw the study-level intercepts from a normal distribution, with a prior on the standard deviation of that normal that is itself a half-normal distribution. # Fixed effects and group specific (or random) intercepts & slopes for study model_slope = bmb. Model("value ~ condition + age + gender + (condition|study)", df_rrr, dropna = True) model_slope. While this model is just meant to be an example (not a proper analysis), the conclusion you might draw from the above is that the results of the original study don’t replicate, and there is *no* effect.
